Question: When a suspect Quoran is noticed to have joined months or even years prior to the first entry in their edit log, is it really a so called “body snatcher account” stolen from a person who died immediately after signing up for Quora?
Answer: It doesn't work that way, Bax Bandacitis. While dormant accounts are sometimes called zombie accounts, it has nothing to do with actual zombies or body snatchers. It just means someone created an account and didn't do anything with it. The account is still technically active, but has no actual activity. It's technically alive but effectively dead. If someone else manages to figure out the account's password, they can take it over and use it for spamming or trolling or other obnoxious sockpuppet activities. For example, they might paste the same shaggy dog story a gazillion times into a single post, and repeat that dozens of times. I guess they decided “Why have turkey on Thanksgiving when you can be one instead?” I can't imagine who might do that or why. Can you?

Question: A queue can be implemented using singly linked list in two ways. One implementation has front at head and rear at tail of the linked list. Other has front at the tail and rear at the head of the linked list. Which implementation is efficient and why?
Answer: Before we get wound up on front, back, head, or tail: the question is really getting at whether the each link in the list should point to an older entry or a younger entry. It suggests there's only two options. There are more than two options; however, I suspect that you were given these two options for a reason. The fact that the question allows the labels front and back to be assigned independently of head and tail also suggests that they haven't locked down their nomenclature. If I look at, say, the C++ standard library, its notion of front and back are pretty unambiguous for std::list and std::forward_list. (The latter is a singly-linked list.) They avoid the terms head and tail. I have seen code bases that swap the meaning of head and tail, so I can understand why the C++ standard library avoids that. In my answer, I will do my best to avoid terms you haven't locked down. And finally, it's not explicitly stated in the question, but let's assume this queue is strictly first-in, first-out (FIFO), as opposed to, say, a priority queue. Thought Experiment Suppose you work in an office with one of those Take-A-Number systems: This is in a budget-strapped office, however, and the system broke down ages ago. The display is broken, and they're reusing the tickets. As people arrive, they draw a random ticket from the box. As people get called, they put their ticket back in the box. That sounds like a real mess, doesn't it? Fortunately, everyone coming to your office is motivated to get in and out efficiently, and nobody there is going to tolerate anyone cutting in line. All the folks in the lobby are willing to help out. What do you ask them to do? Here are some options: Let's walk through these. Option 1 This one is easy for you, at least at first. You just have to remember the ticket number for whoever walked in the door last. When it's time to figure out who to call up next, you ask them for the ticket number of the person before them. Keep doing this until you find the person waiting longest. That's not too bad with 2 or 3 people waiting. I think it gets old pretty quickly, though. On the plus side, as new people arrive, you can quickly say “Hey, remember the guy before you has ticket number X.” Option 2 This feels a little better than option 1, because now each person can you the number of the next person to call. The problem is that when someone new arrives, you don't have any way to help them figure out who arrived just before them. So, you both go down the line asking person by person until you find the end. Ultimately, option 2 doesn't seem much better than option 1, does it? Option 3 Finally, you’ve had enough with options 1 and 2. Then inspiration strikes: if you remember the number for who's been waiting longest, and who arrived most recently, now you can avoid asking all the folks in line what order they're in. When you're done with one person, you can ask them who's next. And when a new person walks in, you can tell the person who was previously at the end of the line that this new person is after them. You just keep track of the two ends of the line. That works pretty well, but now you have two numbers to remember. Option 4 Let's say the stress of working in this underfunded office is starting to get to you, and you can only reliably keep track of one number. How do you cope? You can ask the last guy who enters to keep track of the guy who was waiting longest for you. Now everyone only has one number to remember. When someone new arrives, the guy who was previously at the end tells the new guy the ticket number of who's been waiting longest, and then takes note of the new guy's ticket number. You just have remember who arrived last. When it's time to call the next person, they can tell you the number for who's next or you can ask the guy at the end for that number. When the next person is called, the guy at the end can ask the guy who was just called what ticket number follows him. Analysis If you followed that thought experiment, you probably figured out I was constructing singly linked lists in different ways. If you replace “ticket number” with “pointer” or “reference,” it should be even more obvious. And if you know your data structures, you probably identified some implementation choices one might make to optimize them. Options 1 and 2 correspond to the two options in the question. Both options are equally bad as presented: Here, d is the average queue depth. Option 1 in C code: Option 2 in C code: Since a FIFO has equal numbers of enqueue and dequeue steps, both end up being O ( d n ) , where d is the average queue depth and n is the total number of elements you’re passing through the queue. If d is proportional to n , then processing the entire queue is O ( n 2 ) . If you put all of the elements in the queue before you withdraw any, you're definitely O ( n 2 ) . Option 3 is a straightforward tweak of option 2, and it provides both O ( 1 ) enqueue and O ( 1 ) dequeue. This approach is quite common in the real world. It's so common that option 2 feels like the special case. That said, data structures courses will likely start with option 2 above and walk through an example like this one to justify constructing option 3. With this tweak, processing n elements is O ( n ) , regardless of the average queue depth. The big annoyance with Option 3 is that you now need two pointers to keep track of the two ends of the list. Option 3 in C code: OK, OK. I’ll admit that I don't feel like introducing a structure to manage the two pointers, or working through all the corner cases to ensure I have managed them correctly. It's not really that difficult, but it is tedious. Option 4 is one that I don't see mentioned as often. It manages the singly linked list as a circular list. Now the last node in the list points to the first node rather than holding a null pointer. Some environments such as the Linux kernel make heavy use of circular lists. In Linux's case, those are doubly-linked, however. As with Option 3, enqueue and dequeue are both O ( 1 ) , and processing n elements is O ( n ) . In order to make this work, you need the list pointer to point at the most recently added element in the queue—i.e. the last element . From there you can easily find the first element, as the last element closes the circle by pointing to the first. Option 4 in C code: Nifty, eh? Summary The italicized points in first two bullets above suggest the question you were given is meant as a setup or prompt. Once you discover neither approach works well, you can explore ways to tweak and improve. At least, I hope that's the case. I really hope they aren't teaching you to parrot canned answers by rote. That's what books and Wikipedia are for.¹ Addendum The above assumes linked lists even make sense for what you're trying to do. These days, they rarely do. See Jerry Coffin's answer for more details. And yes, in C++ I really do just use std::vector whenever possible. ¹ Or ChatGPT / Gemini / Poe / etc. if you love having complete BS presented as confidently, clearly, and insipidly as correct information.

Question: Let's say I declare a valid opcode instruction with db in-between other *actual* instructions, like mov, will the processor treat the expression defined with db as an instruction, or just as byte variables? How does the processor know the difference?
Answer: Let me get this straight. You want to do something like this, correct? Here, DB stands for Define Byte or Data Byte. It directly injects the byte 0x2C into the code stream in the example above. Directives such as DB or .byte or similar don't define variables. They just inject bytes into the assembled output. Likewise for their cousins DW and .word. The exact names of the directives will vary by assembler, but in my experience they all follow a similar model. Can the processor tell the difference between this byte and any other 0x2C in memory? No. How would it? The above sequence assembles to the following 5 bytes. Notice there aren't any flags or markers that distinguish opcode bytes from argument bytes from bytes inserted by the DB directive. Bytes are bytes. So what happens when the processor tries to execute this byte I inserted? It treats it as an instruction, just like any other. Invalid Opcodes If I inserted an invalid opcode into code stream here, then what happens next depends on the CPU. The original NMOS 6502 didn't check for invalid opcodes. As a result, it has a number of “undocumented instructions.” I put that in quotes, as their existence is unintentional. These aren’t instructions that were deliberately added but left undocumented.* Some of these invalid opcodes behave like a combination of officially defined instructions. Several are so-called KIL opcodes that hang the chip until the next reset. Links: (*Unlike the 8085’s undocumented V and K flags and associated instructions, which appear to be deliberate, but incompatible with Intel’s 8080 to 8086 forward compatibility story. Link in the comments.) The 6502’s CMOS upgrade—the 65C02—treats invalid opcodes to NOPs. Modern CPUs typically throw invalid opcode exceptions. Older CPUs displayed a mix of behaviors, either ignoring invalid opcodes, or running random operations that just happened to fall out of the implementation. Valid Opcodes If it's a valid opcode, then the processor will execute it just like any other instruction. Now those of you that really know their 6502 may have noticed I’m up to something with my example. And those of you who aren't 6502 experts may have suspected something anyway, if you’ve read enough of my other answers. This is our original assembly code: It assembled to: A disassembler will take object code and display the instruction sequence associated with it. It decodes the instructions in much the same way that the processor would, at least on straight-line code. What do you suppose a disassembler will show us for the 5 bytes of object code above? I suggest you try disassembling this code yourself. I’ll wait while you work it by hand. It's only 5 bytes. There's a nice opcode summary here: Link: http://www.6502.org/tutorials/6502opcodes.html  This image may also help, by mapping bytes to mnemonics: . . . . . . Ready? It disassembles to: Wait, what? What happened to the other LDA? It became part of the BIT instruction! If we start at the first LDA instruction, we’ll end up executing the two instructions you see above—LDA #$42 followed by BIT $47A9. The second LDA is gone! The Liksee (LXI) and Movie (MVI) Tricks What I just showed you is a 6502 version of what's also been called the LXI (“liksee") trick, named for the 8080 LXI instruction. There's a related MVI (“movie”) trick, named for the 8080 MVI instruction. I’ll let Tim Paterson (of MS-DOS fame) explain: Link: https://archive.org/details/dr_dobbs_journal_vol_15/page/215/mode/1up And that's exactly what's happening in my example. I just happened to use BIT, because it only modifies flags and only needs 4 cycles. A relative branch takes 3 cycles, but requires two bytes. This is a size/speed tradeoff. So let's see what's really going on here: If you jump to a, you’ll reach point c with A = $42, because the BIT instruction “swallows” the second LDA. If you jump to b, you’ll reach point c with A = $47. Nifty, eh? The Punchline Bytes are bytes. If you try to execute some bytes you inserted into the code, the processor won't treat those bytes differently from other instructions. With that knowledge in hand, you can do some clever—if somewhat sleazy—tricks. Addendum Note that my answer assumes the OP is injecting one or more bytes between two instructions in otherwise executable code. If you are using a machine with an MMU that can treat some memory regions as executable, and others as non-executable, that doesn't really affect my answer. The instructions involved should already be in an executable region. The data byte will be right in there with them. As I stated: bytes are bytes. They don't have flags or markers on them to flag them individually as data or code. Some MMUs may treat separate regions of memory as executable vs. non-executable, but that's unrelated to the question at hand.
